warmup.q: Limits has static final int MAX_MINOR = 500_000;, static final Integer CAP = 500_000; and a static {} block that prints "init". Another class prints Limits.MAX_MINOR, then Limits.CAP. When does "init" appear?
options: Before the first value, because touching any member of a class initializes it
Between the two values: reading MAX_MINOR doesn't initialize Limits, reading CAP does
Never, because both fields are static final
warmup.why: MAX_MINOR is a constant variable: a static final primitive with a constant initializer. javac copies 500000 into the caller's class file, so the caller never touches Limits at run time. CAP is boxed (Integer.valueOf runs), so it is not a constant, and reading it runs Limits's static initializer. A class initializes at most once, so "init" can't print twice.

sections.h: Every class has a defining loader, and it is part of the class's identity
sections.html:
Your compiled classes sit in jars and directories, and the JVM reads none of them until some code needs one. A class loader is the object that finds a class's bytes and turns them into a Class the JVM can run. Ask three classes who loaded them and you get three different answers:

Java
System.out.println(String.class.getClassLoader());              // null
System.out.println(java.sql.Connection.class.getClassLoader());  // ...ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@<hash>
System.out.println(PaymentApp.class.getClassLoader());          // ...ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@<hash>
Kotlin
println(String::class.java.classLoader)                // null
println(java.sql.Connection::class.java.classLoader)   // ...ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@<hash>
println(PaymentApp::class.java.classLoader)            // ...ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@<hash>

The JDK has three built-in class loaders. The bootstrap loader is part of the JVM and loads java.base; the ClassLoader Javadoc says it is "typically represented as null". The platform loader loads the other Java SE and JDK modules, such as java.sql and java.net.http. The app loader (also called the system loader) loads your class path: your code, Quarkus, the Kafka client, the Kotlin standard library. Each one has the next as its parent: app, then platform, then bootstrap. JDK 21 and JDK 25 print the same chain.

When code asks a loader for a class, the default loadClass does three things in order. It checks whether this loader already has the name (findLoadedClass). If not, it asks its parent, which asks its own parent first. Only when every parent fails does it call its own findClass. So java.lang.String always comes from the bootstrap loader, even if some jar on your class path contains a class with that name. This is parent-first delegation. It's why a stray jar can't replace a JDK class.

The loader that finally calls defineClass is the class's defining loader, and it is part of the class's identity. At run time a class is the pair (binary name, defining loader). The binary name is the full name, such as com.acme.Money, or com.acme.Money$Rate for a nested class. Two loaders that each define com.acme.Money from the same bytes produce two classes that happen to share a name. You'll build exactly that in the lab, and section 4 shows what it does to a cast.

Kotlin adds nothing special here. kotlin.Unit is an ordinary class in an ordinary jar, so the app loader defines it like any other library class.

sections.h: Loading, linking and initialization are three steps, and only the last runs your code
sections.html:
Loading a class and running its static {} block are separate events. Chapter 5 of the JVM specification splits the work into three phases, and HotSpot runs each one as late as it is allowed to.

  1. Loading finds the bytes (in a jar, a directory, or generated in memory) and turns them into a Class object with defineClass.
  2. Linking checks and prepares the class. Verification proves that the bytecode, the instructions the compiler wrote into the class file (lesson 2), is type-safe. Preparation creates the static fields and sets them to their defaults: 0, false, null. Resolution turns symbolic references in the constant pool, the class file's table of the names it uses, ("method charge in class Ledger") into direct ones, and may do it lazily, one reference at a time.
  3. Initialization runs the class's static initializer, which javac names <clinit>: every static field initializer and static {} block, in source order.

Two small experiments show the gaps between the phases. A generated class with broken bytecode was accepted by ClassLoader.defineClass on JDK 25, and the VerifyError appeared only when code first asked for its methods. A class that referenced a deleted Helper class loaded and ran fine. It failed with NoClassDefFoundError only when the branch that used Helper executed.

Initialization is the phase your code can see, and its triggers are precise. JLS section 12.4.1 lists them: creating an instance, calling a static method, assigning a static field, or reading a static field that is not a constant variable. Initializing a class first initializes its superclass. Reflection such as Class.forName(name) or a reflective static field read counts too.

These do not initialize a class:

  • reading a static final primitive or String that has a constant initializer, because javac copied the value into your class file;
  • Limits.class, new Limits[3] and Class.forName(name, false, loader);
  • reading an inherited static field through a subclass name: Child.parentValue initializes only Parent, the class that declares the field.

The constant rule surprises people most. static final int MAX_MINOR = 500_000 is a constant variable. static final Integer CAP = 500_000 is not, because boxing calls Integer.valueOf. Reading the first leaves Limits alone. Reading the second runs <clinit>. Kotlin draws the same line between const val and a plain val.

try.title: The initialization puzzle
steps: Read InitPuzzle (or InitPuzzle.kt). For each of the eight steps, write down whether a <clinit> line prints after it, and which one.
Run it and check your list.

Each <clinit> prints one indented line. */ public class InitPuzzle { static class Parent { static int parentValue = 1; static { System.out.println(" Parent.<clinit>"); } } static class Child extends Parent { static { System.out.println(" Child.<clinit>"); } } static class Limits { static final int MAX_MINOR = 500_000; // a constant variable: javac copies 500000 into callers static final Integer CAP = 500_000; // boxed, so not a constant variable static { System.out.println(" Limits.<clinit>"); } } static class Lazy { static { System.out.println(" Lazy.<clinit>"); } static void touch() {} } interface Step { void run() throws Exception; } static void step(String what, Step s) throws Exception { System.out.println(what); s.run(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { step("1. read Child.parentValue", () -> { int v = Child.parentValue; }); step("2. new Child()", () -> new Child()); step("3. read Limits.MAX_MINOR", () -> { int v = Limits.MAX_MINOR; }); step("4. read Limits.CAP", () -> { Integer v = Limits.CAP; }); step("5. new Lazy[3]", () -> { Lazy[] a = new Lazy[3]; }); step("6. Lazy.class", () -> { Class<?> c = Lazy.class; }); step("7. Class.forName(name, false, loader)", () -> Class.forName("workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzle$Lazy", false, InitPuzzle.class.getClassLoader())); step("8. Lazy.touch()", Lazy::touch); } }

sections.h: A static initializer runs once, top to bottom, under a lock
sections.html:
<clinit> is ordinary code, with three properties that cause real outages.

It runs in source order. In this class the constructor runs before the line that sets DEFAULT_BPS:

Java
public final class FeeSchedule {
    public static final FeeSchedule INSTANCE = new FeeSchedule();   // runs first
    private static final int DEFAULT_BPS =
            Integer.parseInt(System.getProperty("fees.default.bps", "350"));

    private final int fallbackBps = DEFAULT_BPS;                   // still 0 here
}
Kotlin
class FeeSchedule private constructor() {
    val fallbackBps = DEFAULT_BPS                                 // still 0 here

    companion object {
        @JvmField val INSTANCE = FeeSchedule()                    // runs first
        private val DEFAULT_BPS = System.getProperty("fees.default.bps", "350").toInt()
    }
}

The thread running <clinit> may read the class's statics while it is still running, so the constructor sees the default 0. Every unknown country now pays a 0 bps fee, and nothing throws. The JVM did exactly what the source says. With a constant initializer (= 350) the bug disappears, because javac inlines it. That's why this bug tends to arrive the day someone makes a constant configurable. The lab has it for you to fix.

It runs once, and a failure is permanent. If <clinit> throws, the first caller gets ExceptionInInitializerError. The JVM marks the class as failed, and every later use from any thread gets NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class .... It never retries. On JDK 21 the cause of that second error even names the original exception and the thread it happened in. In a long log you often see the NoClassDefFoundError hundreds of times and the real cause once, near the top.

It runs under a lock. One thread runs <clinit> and every other thread that needs the class waits. That lock is what makes the holder idiom from the memory model track safe, and it can deadlock. If FxRates's initializer reads Fees, Fees's initializer reads FxRates, and two threads start one each, each thread holds one class's lock and waits for the other's. The threads report RUNNABLE, not BLOCKED. ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() returns nothing, and jstack prints waiting on the Class initialization monitor for ... with no "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. Search thread dumps for that phrase when a service hangs at startup.

Keep static initializers boring. Constants and small immutable maps are fine. File reads, network calls and reads of other classes' statics belong in a lazy method or in a bean that the container starts.

try.title: Deadlock two classes
steps: Run InitDeadlockDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It starts two threads and waits one second.
Read the state and top frame it prints for each thread, and what the deadlock detector says.
Optional: run it with -Pargs=wait, then run the printed jstack command in a second terminal and search for Class initialization monitor.
Fix it: make Fees.CARD_BPS a constant (static final long CARD_BPS = 108;, or const val in Kotlin) and run again.

code.title: InitDeadlockDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.List; /** Two static initializers that need each other, started from two threads. */ public class InitDeadlockDemo { static class FxRates { static final long EUR_USD; static { pause(); EUR_USD = Fees.CARD_BPS + 108_000; } // needs Fees } static class Fees { static final long CARD_BPS; static { pause(); CARD_BPS = FxRates.EUR_USD / 1_000; } // needs FxRates } static void pause() { try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread a = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(FxRates.EUR_USD), "rates"); Thread b = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Fees.CARD_BPS), "fees"); a.setDaemon(true); // daemon, so the JVM can still exit at the end b.setDaemon(true); a.start(); b.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); for (Thread t : List.of(a, b)) { System.out.printf("%-5s state=%s at %s%n", t.getName(), t.getState(), t.getStackTrace()[0]); } long[] stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); System.out.println("deadlock detector: " + (stuck == null ? "found nothing" : stuck.length + " threads")); if (args.length > 0) { // -Pargs=wait gives you 30 s to run jstack System.out.println("jstack " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " (search for 'Class initialization monitor')"); Thread.sleep(30_000); } } }

alt.title: InitDeadlockDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two objects whose initializers need each other, started from two threads. object KFxRates { @JvmField val EUR_USD: Long init { pausePlease(); EUR_USD = KFees.CARD_BPS + 108_000 } // needs KFees } object KFees { @JvmField val CARD_BPS: Long init { pausePlease(); CARD_BPS = KFxRates.EUR_USD / 1_000 } // needs KFxRates } private fun pausePlease() = Thread.sleep(200) fun main(args: Array<String>) { // daemon threads, so the JVM can still exit at the end val a = thread(name = "rates", isDaemon = true) { println(KFxRates.EUR_USD) } val b = thread(name = "fees", isDaemon = true) { println(KFees.CARD_BPS) } Thread.sleep(1_000) for (t in listOf(a, b)) { println("%-5s state=%s at %s".format(t.name, t.state, t.stackTrace[0])) } val stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() println("deadlock detector: " + (stuck?.let { "${it.size} threads" } ?: "found nothing")) if (args.isNotEmpty()) { // -Pargs=wait gives you 30 s to run jstack println("jstack ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()} (search for 'Class initialization monitor')") Thread.sleep(30_000) } }

try.expect: Both threads show state=RUNNABLE with a top frame inside <clinit>, and the detector prints found nothing. The JVM exits only because the threads are daemons. In jstack each thread is in Object.wait() and waiting on the Class initialization monitor for the other class. After the fix, Fees no longer needs FxRates, so both threads print a number and the program ends normally.

sections.h: Same bytes, two loaders: two classes
sections.html:
Because the loader is part of a class's identity, a custom loader can define its own copy of a class the app loader already has. Plugin systems, application servers and Quarkus dev mode do this on purpose. The usual tool is a child-first loader: for its own package prefix it calls findClass before it asks the parent.

Java
@Override
protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException {
    synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) {
        Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name);
        if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) c = findClass(name);   // child-first
        return c != null ? c : super.loadClass(name, resolve);            // parent-first
    }
}
Kotlin
override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> =
    synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) {
        var c = findLoadedClass(name)
        if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) c = findClass(name)   // child-first
        c ?: super.loadClass(name, resolve)                              // parent-first
    }

Two such loaders over one class file give you two Class objects. Each has its own statics, and its static initializer runs once per loader. An object from one copy can't be cast to the other, even though the names match. The message is long, and worth learning to read:

class ...TwoLoadersDemo$Counter cannot be cast to class ...TwoLoadersDemo$Counter
(...$Counter is in unnamed module of loader 'plugin-1' @606d8acf;
 ...$Counter is in unnamed module of loader 'app')

The same name twice with two loaders means isolation, not a missing jar. The Quarkus class-loading reference describes where you'll meet it: tests and dev mode use several loaders. Your application classes live in a Runtime ClassLoader that is recreated on every hot reload, on top of a Base Runtime ClassLoader that persists. The guide warns that marking a dependency "parent first" without also marking its dependencies can cause a LinkageError. (That comes from the Quarkus docs; this track didn't run dev mode.)

The two "not found" errors fit the same picture. ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception from an explicit lookup by name, such as Class.forName or loadClass. NoClassDefFoundError comes from the JVM while it links or initializes code that was compiled against the class: either the class is missing at run time (the cause is then a ClassNotFoundException), or its static initializer already failed.

Leaks have the same shape. A loader stays alive while anything reachable points at one of its classes or objects. In one experiment, a plugin instance added to a static list in a parent-loaded registry kept its whole URLClassLoader alive after close() and ten System.gc() calls, along with a 10 MB static array. Without the registration, the loader was collected. A persistent cache that holds an object from the previous Runtime ClassLoader pins every class of that old copy in the same way.

try.title: Two Counters that aren't the same class
steps: Read TwoLoadersDemo. It loads Counter through two child-first loaders and calls hit() twice on the copy from plugin-1.
Predict the three hits values and whether the cast at the end works.
Run it (or the Kotlin twin) and find the two loader names in the exception message.

code.title: TwoLoadersDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; /** The same class file defined by two loaders: two classes, two sets of statics. */ public class TwoLoadersDemo { public static class Counter { public static int hits; public int hit() { return ++hits; } } /** Defines Counter itself (child-first); asks the parent for everything else. */ static class ChildFirst extends ClassLoader { ChildFirst(String name) { super(name, TwoLoadersDemo.class.getClassLoader()); } @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException { if (!name.equals(Counter.class.getName())) return super.loadClass(name, resolve); synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) { Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name); if (c != null) return c; try (InputStream in = getParent().getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class")) { byte[] bytes = in.readAllBytes(); return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length); } catch (IOException e) { throw new ClassNotFoundException(name, e); } } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String name = Counter.class.getName(); Class<?> c1 = new ChildFirst("plugin-1").loadClass(name); Class<?> c2 = new ChildFirst("plugin-2").loadClass(name); System.out.println("same name: " + c1.getName().equals(c2.getName())); System.out.println("c1 == c2: " + (c1 == c2) + ", c1 == Counter.class: " + (c1 == Counter.class)); Object fromPlugin1 = c1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1); c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1); System.out.printf("hits: plugin-1=%s, plugin-2=%s, app=%s%n", c1.getField("hits").get(null), c2.getField("hits").get(null), Counter.hits); try { Counter c = (Counter) fromPlugin1; // checkcast against the app loader's Counter } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); } } }

alt.title: TwoLoadersDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01 class KCounter { fun hit(): Int = ++hits companion object { @JvmField var hits = 0 } } /** Defines KCounter itself (child-first); asks the parent for everything else. */ private class KChildFirst(name: String) : ClassLoader(name, KCounter::class.java.classLoader) { override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> { if (name != KCounter::class.java.name) return super.loadClass(name, resolve) synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) { findLoadedClass(name)?.let { return it } val bytes = parent.getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class")!!.use { it.readAllBytes() } return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.size) } } } /** The same class file defined by two loaders: two classes, two sets of statics. */ fun main() { val name = KCounter::class.java.name val c1 = KChildFirst("plugin-1").loadClass(name) val c2 = KChildFirst("plugin-2").loadClass(name) println("same name: ${c1.name == c2.name}") println("c1 == c2: ${c1 == c2}, c1 == KCounter::class.java: ${c1 == KCounter::class.java}") val fromPlugin1 = c1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() repeat(2) { c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1) } println("hits: plugin-1=${c1.getField("hits").get(null)}, plugin-2=${c2.getField("hits").get(null)}, app=${KCounter.hits}") try { val c = fromPlugin1 as KCounter // checkcast against the app loader's KCounter } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println(e.message) } }

try.expect: same name: true, c1 == c2: false and c1 == Counter.class: false. The hits are plugin-1=2, plugin-2=0, app=0: three classes, three separate static fields. The cast fails with ... cannot be cast to class ...$Counter, and the parentheses name loader 'plugin-1' and loader 'app'.

analogy: A class name is like an account number, and the defining loader is the bank. Account 4471 at two banks is two accounts with two balances, and a transfer form for one bank rejects the other bank's account even though the numbers match. Parent-first delegation is a branch that always asks head office whether it already holds the account before it opens a new one, so nobody can open a second "java.lang.String". The analogy breaks in one place: two copies of a class are not strangers. They come from the same bytes and share everything their parent loaded, such as String and the interfaces they implement, which is why a plugin can still be used through a shared interface.
world: Picture an FX service that loads its rate table in a static initializer: static final RateTable RATES = RateTable.load(Path.of("rates.csv")). In a Quarkus test run the file isn't on the test path. The first test fails with ExceptionInInitializerError, and the next forty fail with NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class RateTable, which sends people looking for a missing dependency. The same class under Quarkus dev mode is defined again by a fresh Runtime ClassLoader on every reload, so a static cache in a parent-first library that keeps old RateTable objects pins the old classes in memory. Load data in a bean that the container starts, and keep statics to constants.
mistake: The common mistake is reading NoClassDefFoundError as "a jar is missing" and adding dependencies until it goes away. Often the jar is fine: the class's static initializer threw once, earlier, and the JVM now refuses that class for the life of its loader. People make this mistake because the later error is the one that fills the log, and its name sounds like a class-path problem. The fix is to search the log for the first ExceptionInInitializerError (or read the cause of the NoClassDefFoundError on JDK 21 and later), fix what threw, and move I/O and configuration out of static initializers into lazy or container-managed code.

compare.title: When static initialization runs, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Limits.java
java.html: class Limits { static final int MAX_MINOR = 500_000; // constant: copied into callers, no init static final Integer CAP = 500_000; // not a constant: reading it runs <clinit> static Limits defaults() { return new Limits(); } static { System.out.println("Limits init"); } } // Limits.MAX_MINOR -> nothing // Limits.CAP -> "Limits init" // Limits.defaults() -> "Limits init" (if not done yet)

kotlin.title: Limits.kt
kotlin.html: object Limits { const val MAX_MINOR = 500_000 // constant: copied into callers, no init val CAP: Int = 500_000 // private static field + getCAP() on the object fun defaults() = Limits init { println("Limits init") } } // Limits.MAX_MINOR -> nothing // Limits.CAP -> "Limits init" (goes through Limits.INSTANCE) // Limits.defaults() -> "Limits init" (if not done yet)

compare.note: Kotlin has no static, but an object compiles to a class with a public static final INSTANCE field and a static initializer that builds it, so the JVM rules are the same. Only const val (primitives and String) is inlined into callers like a Java constant variable. A plain val in an object becomes a private static field plus a getter, so reading it touches the class and runs its init blocks. Companion objects follow the same rules, and their init code lands in the outer class's static {} block, which is why the Kotlin FeeSchedule in section 3 reads 0 exactly like the Java one.

worked.title: Read a NoClassDefFoundError back to its cause

steps.say: A Quarkus test run shows this, forty times. Before reading on, decide: is a jar missing?
steps.code:
java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class com.acme.fx.RateTable
    at com.acme.fx.QuoteService.quote(QuoteService.java:31)
    ...
Caused by: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError: Exception java.lang.IllegalStateException:
    rates file missing: rates.csv [in thread "executor-thread-1"]

steps.say: No. "Could not initialize class" means the JVM found RateTable and already tried to initialize it. The cause (JDK 21 and later) points at the first failure. Here is the class. Each chunk of <clinit> runs once, in order.
steps.code: public final class RateTable { // 1. runs inside <clinit>: any exception here poisons the class for good static final RateTable CURRENT = load(Path.of("rates.csv")); static RateTable load(Path p) { if (!Files.exists(p)) throw new IllegalStateException("rates file missing: " + p); return new RateTable(/* parse 4,000 lines */); } }

alt.html: class RateTable private constructor() { companion object { // 1. runs inside RateTable's <clinit>: any exception here poisons the class for good val CURRENT: RateTable = load(Path.of("rates.csv")) fun load(p: Path): RateTable { check(Files.exists(p)) { "rates file missing: $p" } return RateTable(/* parse 4,000 lines */) } } }

steps.say: Move the I/O out of class initialization. A bean the container builds at startup fails once, with a clear stack trace, and a fixed file or a restart of the test fixes it. The class itself has no static state left to poison.
steps.code: @ApplicationScoped public class RateTableProvider { private volatile RateTable current; @PostConstruct void load() { // 2. ordinary code, ordinary exception current = RateTable.load(Path.of("rates.csv")); } public RateTable current() { return current; } // 3. no static state left to poison }

alt.html: @ApplicationScoped class RateTableProvider { @Volatile private lateinit var current: RateTable @PostConstruct fun load() { // 2. ordinary code, ordinary exception current = RateTable.load(Path.of("rates.csv")) } fun current(): RateTable = current // 3. no static state left to poison }

steps.say: If the value must stay static, make it lazy with a holder class (memory model track, lesson 5). A failure still poisons the holder, but only callers that need the table see it, and the error appears at the first real use instead of whenever some unrelated class touched RateTable.

lab.title: Fix an initialization-order bug, then load one class twice
steps: Run the tests once. Eight of ten fail: the unknown-country fee comes back as 0, and every loader test hits UnsupportedOperationException.

In FeeSchedule, read the static fields from top to bottom as <clinit> runs them. Move one line so the constructor sees the real DEFAULT_BPS. Don't change any number. Ask yourself why currency() was right all along.

In IsolatingLoader.findClass, read the class file through the parent with getParent().getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class"), then call defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length). Throw ClassNotFoundException when the stream is null.

In loadClass, take getClassLoadingLock(name). Return findLoadedClass(name) if it isn't null. For names that start with the prefix, call findClass. For everything else, return super.loadClass(name, resolve).
Run the tests until all ten pass. Then read castAcrossLoadersFails and find which loader names appear in the message.
hints: Constants such as "EUR" are inlined by javac, so their order doesn't matter. Integer.parseInt(...) is a method call, so DEFAULT_BPS is 0 until <clinit> reaches its line.
If a test fails with LinkageError: attempted duplicate class definition, your loadClass defined the same name twice. Check findLoadedClass first.
Don't call super.loadClass for prefix names before findClass: the parent would find the app's copy and you'd get the same Class from both loaders.

drill.title: A child-first loader from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page and the lab. Write loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) for a loader that defines classes under prefix itself and delegates everything else to its parent. Then check: did you take the class-loading lock, and did you look for an already-loaded class before defining one?

answer.html: @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException { synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) { Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name); // 1. defined here already? if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) { c = findClass(name); // 2. child-first for the plugin } if (c == null) return super.loadClass(name, resolve); // 3. parent-first for the rest if (resolve) resolveClass(c); return c; } }

alt.html: override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> = synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) { var c = findLoadedClass(name) // 1. defined here already? if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) { c = findClass(name) // 2. child-first for the plugin } if (c == null) return super.loadClass(name, resolve) // 3. parent-first for the rest if (resolve) resolveClass(c) c }

recap: Three built-in loaders: bootstrap (null, java.base), platform (other JDK modules), app (your class path). They delegate parent-first.
A class is (binary name, defining loader). The same bytes defined by two loaders are two classes with separate statics, and casts between them fail.
Loading, linking (verify, prepare, resolve) and initialization are separate and lazy. Only initialization runs <clinit>.
Initialization triggers: new, a static call, a non-constant static read or write, reflection, a subclass. Constants, X.class, arrays and forName(n, false, l) don't trigger it.

<clinit> runs once, in source order, under a lock. A throw gives ExceptionInInitializerError once, then NoClassDefFoundError forever. Two initializers that need each other can deadlock with both threads RUNNABLE.
ClassNotFoundException is an explicit lookup failing. NoClassDefFoundError is the JVM failing to link or initialize a class your code was compiled against.

explain.prompt: A teammate sees NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class FeeSchedule in production and wants to add fees-core.jar to the image. Explain what the error really says, how you'd find the cause, and how to stop it happening again.
explain.answer: The JVM found FeeSchedule fine. It already tried to run its static initializer once, that initializer threw, and the JVM marked the class as failed, so every later use gets NoClassDefFoundError and it never retries. Adding a jar won't help. I'd look for the first ExceptionInInitializerError in the log, or read the cause chain, which on JDK 21 names the original exception and thread. The fix is whatever made the initializer throw, plus moving that work out of <clinit>: keep statics to constants and do I/O or configuration in a bean the container starts or in a lazy holder, so a failure is an ordinary exception at the call that needs it.

deeper.html:
Three details that didn't fit above.

Interfaces have their own initialization rule. Initializing a class initializes its superclass, but its superinterfaces only if they declare a default method. In one experiment, new Impl() for a class implementing WithDefault (which has a default method) and NoDefault (which doesn't) printed WithDefault.<clinit> and Impl.<clinit>, and NoDefault stayed uninitialized until code read one of its fields. HotSpot's InstanceKlass::initialize_impl follows the JVMS steps one by one, and its comments quote this rule.

Lambdas are hidden classes. A lambda's class has a name like LoaderInfo$$Lambda/0x00007f2408000a08, isHidden() returns true, and Class.forName on that name throws ClassNotFoundException. LambdaMetafactory defines it with Lookup.defineHiddenClass (JDK 15) as a nestmate of the class that contains the lambda, which means it may use that class's private members. Lesson 3 of this track shows the call site that creates it.

You can watch the phases. -Xlog:class+load=info prints a line per loaded class with its source, and -Xlog:class+init=info prints verification start and end and an Initializing '...' line per class. A Hello World with one lambda loaded 560 classes on JDK 21 and 645 on JDK 25, most of them from the CDS archive (source: shared objects file), a file of JDK classes that were already parsed when the JDK was built. The startup track covers that archive and the AOT cache that JDK 24 and 25 build on it.

java -Xlog:class+load=info -Xlog:class+init=info -cp bytecode/build/classes/java/demo workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzle | grep -E 'InitPuzzle|Initializing'
